api-rest.tldr:
• Resources are nouns; methods have defined safety and idempotency (PUT/DELETE idempotent, POST not).
  • Use status codes deliberately: 201 + Location, 202 for async, 409, 412, 422, 429 with Retry-After.
  • Never return 200 with an error body.
  • Allowlist and index filter and sort fields; cap page sizes.
api-rest.body:
Resources are nouns; HTTP methods are the verbs.

HTTP
GET    /api/v1/orders?status=PAID&sort=-createdAt&limit=20    list (filter, sort, paginate)
POST   /api/v1/orders                                          create      -> 201 Created + Location
GET    /api/v1/orders/42                                       read one
PUT    /api/v1/orders/42                                       replace whole resource
PATCH  /api/v1/orders/42                                       partial update
DELETE /api/v1/orders/42                                       delete      -> 204 No Content
GET    /api/v1/customers/7/orders                              sub-collection (ownership is clear)
POST   /api/v1/orders/42/cancellation                          an action modelled as a resource

Guidelines: plural collection names, lowercase-hyphenated paths, no verbs in paths (/getOrders ✗), nest at most one level (/customers/7/orders, not /customers/7/orders/42/items/3/reviews), JSON field names consistent (camelCase or snake_case, pick one), ISO-8601 timestamps in UTC, amounts as integer minor units or decimal strings with a currency.

A resource model for an order API

Keep nesting to one level (/customers/{id}/orders), expose every entity at a top-level path too (/orders/{id}), and model actions that don't fit CRUD as sub-resources (cancellation, refunds) instead of verbs in the URL (/cancelOrder).

Method semantics — know this table cold

Method Safe (no side effects) Idempotent (repeat = same effect) Body Typical success
GET yes yes no 200
HEAD yes yes no 200 (headers only)
OPTIONS yes yes no 204 / 200 (CORS preflight)
PUT no yes full resource 200 / 204, or 201 if created
DELETE no yes usually none 204 (repeat: 204 or 404)
POST no no yes 201 + Location, 200, or 202
PATCH no not guaranteed partial changes 200 / 204

Idempotency matters because clients and proxies retry. Retrying a PUT or DELETE is safe; retrying a POST may create duplicates unless you add an idempotency key (see the idempotency guide).

PATCH formats: JSON Merge Patch (RFC 7396, application/merge-patch+json) sends the fields to change and null to remove; JSON Patch (RFC 6902) sends operations ([{"op":"replace","path":"/status","value":"SHIPPED"}]). Merge Patch is simpler; JSON Patch can express array edits.

Safe, idempotent, cacheable — at a glance

Status codes you should use deliberately

Code Meaning Use for
200 OK success with body GET, PUT/PATCH returning the resource
201 Created resource created POST that created something; include Location
202 Accepted accepted for async processing long-running jobs; return a status URL
204 No Content success, no body DELETE, PUT without a response body
301 / 308 permanent redirect (308 keeps the method) moved endpoints
304 Not Modified cached copy still valid conditional GET with If-None-Match
400 Bad Request malformed request unparseable JSON, wrong types
401 Unauthorized not authenticated missing/expired/invalid token; send WWW-Authenticate
403 Forbidden authenticated but not allowed lacks role/permission
404 Not Found no such resource (or you won't reveal it) also for resources the caller may not know exist
405 Method Not Allowed method unsupported on this path include Allow header
409 Conflict state conflict duplicate unique value, invalid state transition, idempotency key in progress
412 Precondition Failed If-Match didn't match optimistic concurrency failure
415 Unsupported Media Type wrong Content-Type XML sent to a JSON API
422 Unprocessable Content well-formed but semantically invalid validation failures (some APIs use 400 for these too; be consistent)
429 Too Many Requests rate limited include Retry-After
500 Internal Server Error unexpected server bug never for client mistakes
502 / 503 / 504 bad gateway / unavailable / gateway timeout dependency failures, overload (Retry-After on 503), upstream timeouts

Pitfall returning 200 OK with {"success": false} breaks every client, proxy, monitor and retry policy that relies on status codes. Use the status code, then put details in the body.

Filtering, sorting and field selection

HTTP
GET /api/v1/orders?status=PAID&createdAfter=2026-10-01T00:00:00Z&sort=-createdAt,id&fields=id,total,status&limit=50

Whitelist sortable and filterable fields (they must be indexed), cap limit, and reject unknown parameters or ignore them consistently.

api-errors.tldr:
• Use RFC 9457 Problem Details (application/problem+json) with stable type URIs.
  • Give every error a machine-readable code and a trace id.
  • Never leak stack traces or internals.
  • Map exceptions centrally; list all validation errors at once.
api-errors.body:
A consistent error format is part of your API contract. RFC 9457 Problem Details (which replaced RFC 7807) is the standard: Content-Type: application/problem+json with these members.

HTTP
HTTP/1.1 422 Unprocessable Content
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{
  "type": "https://api.shop.example/problems/validation-failed",
  "title": "Your request has invalid fields",
  "status": 422,
  "detail": "2 fields failed validation",
  "instance": "/api/v1/orders",
  "traceId": "4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736",
  "errors": [
    { "field": "items[0].quantity", "code": "must_be_positive", "message": "must be greater than 0" },
    { "field": "notifyEmail", "code": "invalid_email", "message": "must be a well-formed email address" }
  ]
}
Member Purpose
type a stable URI identifying the problem type; clients branch on this, not on title text
title short human summary of the type
status HTTP status, duplicated for convenience
detail explanation specific to this occurrence
instance URI of this occurrence or the request path
extensions any extra fields: errors, traceId, balance, retryAfter…

Choosing the status code

Rules

  • Machine-readable codes for every error (insufficient_funds, order_already_shipped); messages can change, codes can't.
  • Include a trace/correlation id so support can find the logs.
  • Never leak internals: no stack traces, SQL, class names or hostnames in responses. Log them server-side with the trace id.
  • Validation errors list all failing fields at once, with paths.
  • Map exceptions to responses in one place (@RestControllerAdvice returning ProblemDetail, shown in the Spring Boot track). Spring Boot can also produce Problem Details for framework errors with spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true.
Java
// Domain exception carrying a stable code -> one handler maps all of them
public class BusinessException extends RuntimeException {
    private final HttpStatus status; private final String code;
    public BusinessException(HttpStatus status, String code, String message) { super(message); this.status = status; this.code = code; }
    public HttpStatus status() { return status; }
    public String code() { return code; }
}

@RestControllerAdvice
class ProblemHandler {
    @ExceptionHandler(BusinessException.class)
    ProblemDetail business(BusinessException ex, HttpServletRequest req) {
        ProblemDetail pd = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(ex.status(), ex.getMessage());
        pd.setType(URI.create("https://api.shop.example/problems/" + ex.code().replace('_', '-')));
        pd.setTitle(ex.code());
        pd.setInstance(URI.create(req.getRequestURI()));
        pd.setProperty("traceId", MDC.get("traceId"));
        return pd;
    }
}
// throw new BusinessException(HttpStatus.CONFLICT, "order_already_shipped", "Order 42 has already shipped");

api-pagination.tldr:
• Cursor pagination is constant-cost and stable; offset allows page jumps but degrades.
  • Use opaque cursors encoding the last sort key; fetch limit + 1 to compute hasMore.
  • Bulk endpoints should report per-item results and cap batch size.
  • Long-running work returns 202 with a status resource or webhooks.

api-idempotency.tldr:
• Idempotency keys make unsafe requests retry-safe: store key + request hash + response.
  • Same key, different body → 422; still in progress → 409; completed → replay.
  • ETags with If-Match give optimistic concurrency (412 on conflict).
  • Cache-Control, ETag and If-None-Match save bandwidth and server work.
api-idempotency.body:
Idempotency keys for unsafe operations. Networks fail after the server processed a request but before the client got the response; the client retries. For POST /payments, that must not charge twice.

The client generates a unique key per logical operation and sends Idempotency-Key: 8e03978e-40d5-43e8-bc93-6894a57f9324 (header described in an IETF HTTP API working group draft and used by Stripe, Adyen and others).

Server algorithm:

  1. Look up the key (scoped to the caller). If a completed record exists and the request body hash matches → return the stored response (same status and body).
  2. Same key, different body → 422 (key reused for another request).
  3. Same key, still in progress → 409 Conflict (client should retry later).
  4. New key → insert a record (status IN_PROGRESS, request hash) atomically via a unique constraint, process, store the response, mark COMPLETED.
  5. Expire records after a retention window (24 h – 7 days).
Java
@Transactional
public ResponseEntity<PaymentResponse> create(String key, String clientId, PaymentRequest req) {
    String hash = sha256(json(req));
    Optional<IdemRecord> existing = idem.findByClientIdAndKey(clientId, key);
    if (existing.isPresent()) {
        IdemRecord r = existing.get();
        if (!r.requestHash().equals(hash)) throw new BusinessException(UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY, "idempotency_key_reused", "Key used with a different request");
        if (r.inProgress()) throw new BusinessException(CONFLICT, "request_in_progress", "Original request still processing");
        return ResponseEntity.status(r.status()).body(r.body(PaymentResponse.class));    // replay
    }
    idem.insertInProgress(clientId, key, hash);          // unique (client_id, key): a concurrent twin fails here
    PaymentResponse res = payments.charge(req);
    idem.complete(clientId, key, 201, res);
    return ResponseEntity.status(201).body(res);
}

(If the side effect is outside your database, e.g. a call to a payment provider, pass your own idempotency key downstream too, and reconcile IN_PROGRESS records that never completed.)

Optimistic concurrency with ETags. Prevent "lost updates" between two clients editing the same resource:

HTTP
GET /api/v1/orders/42
200 OK
ETag: "v17"

PUT /api/v1/orders/42
If-Match: "v17"
...body...
-> 200 OK, ETag: "v18"         when the version still matches
-> 412 Precondition Failed      when someone else updated it first (client re-fetches and retries)

Require If-Match on updates (428 Precondition Required when missing) for resources that are edited concurrently. Map the ETag to the JPA @Version column.

HTTP caching headers

Header Purpose
Cache-Control: public, max-age=300 shared caches/CDNs may store for 5 minutes
Cache-Control: private, no-cache only the browser may store, and must revalidate each time
Cache-Control: no-store never store (personal or sensitive data)
ETag + If-None-Match revalidation: server returns 304 Not Modified with no body if unchanged
Last-Modified + If-Modified-Since time-based revalidation
Vary: Accept-Encoding, Authorization cache key must include these request headers

Spring offers ShallowEtagHeaderFilter (hashes the response body; saves bandwidth, not server work) or explicit ResponseEntity.ok().eTag(...).cacheControl(CacheControl.maxAge(...)) for real savings.

api-versioning.tldr:
• Additive changes are compatible; removing, renaming or retyping fields is not.
  • Version in the URI (most common), header/media type, or by date.
  • Announce retirement with Deprecation and Sunset headers.
  • OpenAPI diff checks and consumer-driven contracts catch breaking changes in CI.
api-versioning.body:
The best version is no new version: evolve compatibly.

Change Compatible?
Add an optional request field yes
Add a response field yes, if clients ignore unknown fields (tolerant reader)
Add a new endpoint or enum value usually (enum: only if clients handle unknown values)
Remove or rename a field no
Change a field's type or meaning no
Make an optional field required no
Tighten validation no (old clients start failing)
Change error codes / status codes no

Configure Jackson to tolerate unknown properties on clients (FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES=false; Spring Boot's default ObjectMapper already disables it), and treat enums as open sets.

Compatible vs breaking changes

Change Compatible?
add an optional request field / response field ✓ (clients must ignore unknown fields — tolerant reader)
add a new endpoint, a new optional query parameter ✓
add an enum value ⚠ breaks clients that switch exhaustively — document "unknown values may appear"
make an optional field required, remove or rename a field ✗
change a type (id number → string) or format (date pattern) ✗
change status codes or error formats ✗
change default sorting / pagination size ⚠ behavioural break

When you must break compatibility

Strategy Example Notes
URI version /api/v2/orders most visible and cache-friendly; the common choice
Header / media type Accept: application/vnd.shop.v2+json cleaner URLs, harder to test in a browser
Query parameter ?version=2 simple, easy to forget
Date-based versions Stripe-Version: 2026-09-30 per-client pinning, gradual upgrades

Run versions side by side, migrate consumers, then retire the old one with notice: the Deprecation response header (RFC 9745) marks an endpoint as deprecated, and the Sunset header (RFC 8594) announces the date it will stop working, plus a Link to migration docs.

Contract-first with OpenAPI

YAML
openapi: 3.1.0
info: { title: Orders API, version: 1.4.0 }
paths:
  /api/v1/orders/{id}:
    get:
      operationId: getOrder
      parameters:
        - { name: id, in: path, required: true, schema: { type: integer, format: int64 } }
      responses:
        "200": { description: The order, content: { application/json: { schema: { $ref: "#/components/schemas/Order" } } } }
        "404": { description: Not found, content: { application/problem+json: { schema: { $ref: "#/components/schemas/Problem" } } } }

Generate server stubs and clients (openapi-generator), or generate the spec from code (springdoc-openapi) and publish it. Catch breaking changes in CI with an OpenAPI diff tool, and protect consumers with consumer-driven contract tests (Pact, Spring Cloud Contract): consumers publish what they rely on, and the provider's build verifies it.

api-grpc.tldr:
• REST for public/browser APIs and caching; gRPC for internal low-latency typed calls; GraphQL for client-shaped graphs.
  • Never reuse protobuf field numbers; mark removed ones reserved.
  • Always set gRPC deadlines; balance load at L7 or client-side.
  • SSE for server-to-client streams; WebSockets for bidirectional, with a pub/sub backplane.
api-grpc.body:
REST/JSON gRPC GraphQL WebSocket / SSE
Transport HTTP/1.1 or 2 HTTP/2 HTTP (usually POST) persistent connection
Payload JSON (text) Protobuf (binary, schema) JSON, client-shaped any (WS) / text events (SSE)
Contract OpenAPI (optional) .proto (required) schema (required) ad hoc
Streaming no (chunked/SSE aside) client, server, bidirectional subscriptions yes (WS bidirectional, SSE server→client)
Browser support native needs gRPC-Web proxy native native
Caching HTTP caches/CDNs none built in hard (POST) n/a
Best for public APIs, CRUD, broad compatibility internal service-to-service, low latency, polyglot many clients needing different shapes of a graph (mobile/web BFF) live updates, chat, dashboards

gRPC essentials

Call type Shape Example
Unary request → response GetOrder
Server streaming request → stream of responses live order status updates
Client streaming stream of requests → response upload telemetry batch
Bidirectional both stream independently chat, real-time bidding
Protobuf
syntax = "proto3";
package shop.inventory.v1;
option java_multiple_files = true;

service InventoryService {
  rpc GetStock (GetStockRequest) returns (StockLevel);
  rpc WatchStock (WatchStockRequest) returns (stream StockLevel);    // server streaming
}
message GetStockRequest { string sku = 1; }
message StockLevel {
  string sku = 1;
  int32 available = 2;
  reserved 3;                    // a removed field's number: never reuse it
  string warehouse = 4;
}
  • Field numbers are the wire contract: never change or reuse them; mark removed ones reserved. Adding fields is compatible.
  • Always set deadlines (stub.withDeadlineAfter(300, MILLISECONDS)); deadlines propagate across hops so downstream work stops when the caller gave up.
  • gRPC status codes (UNAVAILABLE, DEADLINE_EXCEEDED, NOT_FOUND, RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED…) replace HTTP codes; only retry UNAVAILABLE (and idempotent calls).
  • Load balancing needs care: HTTP/2 multiplexes many calls on one long-lived connection, so L4 balancers pin all traffic to one backend. Use client-side balancing or an L7 proxy/mesh (Envoy, Linkerd).

GraphQL essentials: clients ask for exactly the fields they need in one round trip. The classic server problem is N+1 resolvers (a list of 50 orders each resolving customer separately) — solved by batching with DataLoader (@BatchMapping in Spring for GraphQL). Protect the server with query depth/complexity limits, persisted queries, and per-field authorization.

WebSocket vs Server-Sent Events: SSE is one-way server→client over plain HTTP with automatic reconnection and Last-Event-ID resume — ideal for notifications, progress and live feeds. WebSockets are bidirectional (chat, collaborative editing, games) but need sticky routing or a pub/sub backplane (Redis, Kafka) to fan out across instances.

Java
// Server-Sent Events in Spring MVC
@GetMapping(path = "/api/v1/orders/{id}/events", produces = MediaType.TEXT_EVENT_STREAM_VALUE)
public SseEmitter orderEvents(@PathVariable long id) {
    SseEmitter emitter = new SseEmitter(Duration.ofMinutes(5).toMillis());
    orderEvents.subscribe(id, evt -> {
        try { emitter.send(SseEmitter.event().id(evt.id()).name(evt.type()).data(evt)); }
        catch (IOException e) { emitter.completeWithError(e); }
    });
    emitter.onCompletion(() -> orderEvents.unsubscribe(id));
    return emitter;
}

api-authn.tldr:
• Sessions are easy to revoke but need CSRF protection; bearer tokens suit APIs.
  • Use Authorization Code + PKCE for user apps and Client Credentials for services; Implicit and ROPC are deprecated.
  • OIDC adds ID tokens for authentication on top of OAuth 2.0.
  • For SPAs, keep tokens server-side in a BFF and give the browser an HttpOnly cookie.
api-authn.body:
Authentication proves who the caller is; authorization decides what they may do.

Sessions vs tokens

Server session (cookie with session id) Bearer token (JWT access token)
State server stores session (Redis for many instances) self-contained, verified by signature
Revocation delete the session: instant hard until expiry (short TTL, deny-list)
Size tiny cookie larger header
CSRF exposure yes (browser sends cookies automatically) → need CSRF protection no, if sent in the Authorization header
Best for server-rendered web apps, BFFs APIs, mobile apps, service-to-service

OAuth 2.0 roles: resource owner (the user), client (the app), authorization server (Keycloak, Okta, Auth0, Cognito, Azure AD), resource server (your API). OAuth is about delegated authorization (access tokens); OpenID Connect (OIDC) adds authentication on top: an ID token (a JWT about the user) and a userinfo endpoint.

Which flow?

Flow Use when Notes
Authorization Code + PKCE any app with a user: SPA, mobile, server-side web the default; PKCE is required by OAuth 2.1 for all clients
Client Credentials service-to-service (no user) client authenticates with a secret, private-key JWT or mTLS
Device Authorization TVs, CLIs without a browser user approves on another device
Refresh Token get new access tokens without re-login rotate refresh tokens; bind to the client
~~Implicit~~, ~~Password (ROPC)~~ — deprecated; removed in OAuth 2.1

PKCE stops an attacker who intercepts the authorization code from exchanging it, because they don't have the code_verifier. The state parameter protects the redirect against CSRF.

Where should a browser app keep tokens? Tokens in localStorage are readable by any XSS. The recommended pattern for SPAs is a Backend-for-Frontend (BFF): the BFF does the OAuth flow, keeps tokens server-side, and gives the browser an HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite session cookie. Spring Security (oauth2Login()) plus Spring Cloud Gateway's TokenRelay filter implements this.

Scopes vs roles: scopes (orders:read) express what the client is allowed to do on the user's behalf; roles/permissions express what the user may do. APIs usually check both: @PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('SCOPE_orders:write') and @orderAuthz.canEdit(#id, authentication)").

api-jwt.tldr:
• JWT payloads are readable; never store secrets in them.
  • Validate signature via JWKS, an allowlisted alg, issuer, audience, exp/nbf.
  • Keep access tokens short-lived; rotate refresh tokens; use deny-lists for emergencies.
  • Asymmetric algorithms (RS256/ES256) let many services verify without sharing a secret.
api-jwt.body:
A JWT is base64url(header).base64url(payload).base64url(signature).

JSON
// header
{ "alg": "RS256", "typ": "JWT", "kid": "2026-10-key-1" }
// payload (claims)
{
  "iss": "https://auth.shop.example/realms/shop",
  "sub": "user-8b1f",
  "aud": "orders-api",
  "exp": 1792660000, "iat": 1792659100, "nbf": 1792659100,
  "scope": "orders:read orders:write",
  "jti": "c2a1f0de-..."
}

The payload is encoded, not encrypted: anyone holding the token can read it. Never put secrets or sensitive personal data in it (use JWE if you truly need encryption).

Signing algorithms

Algorithm Key Use when
HS256 (HMAC) one shared secret signs and verifies a single service issues and verifies its own tokens
RS256 / PS256 (RSA) private key signs, public key verifies an auth server issues tokens many services verify
ES256 / EdDSA elliptic-curve key pair same as RSA, with smaller keys and signatures

Resource servers fetch public keys from the issuer's JWKS endpoint and pick the right one by kid, which allows key rotation without downtime.

What the resource server does with each request

Validation checklist for a resource server

  1. Signature valid with a key from the trusted issuer's JWKS.
  2. alg is on your allowlist (never accept none; never let a token choose HMAC when you expect RSA — the classic algorithm confusion attack uses the public key as an HMAC secret).
  3. iss equals the expected issuer.
  4. aud contains your API (a token minted for another service must not work on yours).
  5. exp in the future, nbf/iat not in the future (allow ~30–60 s clock skew).
  6. Required scopes/roles present for this endpoint.
Java
@Configuration
@EnableMethodSecurity
class ResourceServerConfig {

    @Bean
    SecurityFilterChain api(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        return http
            .csrf(c -> c.disable())                                   // bearer tokens in headers: no CSRF exposure
            .sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
            .authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a
                .requestMatchers("/actuator/health/**").permitAll()
                .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/api/v1/orders/**").hasAuthority("SCOPE_orders:read")
                .requestMatchers("/api/v1/orders/**").hasAuthority("SCOPE_orders:write")
                .anyRequest().authenticated())
            .oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()))
            .build();
    }

    @Bean
    JwtDecoder jwtDecoder(@Value("${spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri}") String issuer) {
        NimbusJwtDecoder decoder = JwtDecoders.fromIssuerLocation(issuer);       // discovers the JWKS, checks iss
        OAuth2TokenValidator<Jwt> audience =
            new JwtClaimValidator<List<String>>(JwtClaimNames.AUD, aud -> aud != null && aud.contains("orders-api"));
        decoder.setJwtValidator(new DelegatingOAuth2TokenValidator<>(JwtValidators.createDefaultWithIssuer(issuer), audience));
        return decoder;
    }
}

Lifetimes and revocation: access tokens short (5–15 min); refresh tokens longer, rotated on every use (reuse of an old refresh token signals theft → revoke the family). For emergency revocation of access tokens: a deny-list of jti values in Redis until their exp, or use opaque tokens with introspection for high-risk APIs.

Service-to-service: client-credentials tokens with an audience per target service, or mTLS (often via a service mesh) proving workload identity; propagate the user's identity downstream with token exchange (RFC 8693) rather than forwarding the user's token to services it wasn't issued for.

Common JWT mistakes: long-lived access tokens; skipping aud checks; trusting the alg header; putting roles that change often into long-lived tokens; storing tokens in localStorage; logging full tokens.

api-owasp.tldr:
• Broken access control (IDOR) is #1: scope every lookup to the caller or tenant.
  • Parameterize all queries; allowlist identifiers like sort columns.
  • Block SSRF by allowlisting hosts and rejecting private and metadata IPs after resolution.
  • Avoid unsafe deserialization, disable XML DTDs, lock down actuator endpoints, scan dependencies.

api-web.tldr:
• CORS is browser-enforced: allowlist explicit origins; never reflect origins with credentials.
  • CSRF matters for cookie-based auth; bearer-token APIs aren't exposed.
  • Session cookies: Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite, optionally the __Host- prefix.
  • Send HSTS, CSP, nosniff and a referrer policy.

api-secrets.tldr:
• Hash passwords with Argon2id, scrypt or bcrypt — never fast hashes or encryption.
  • Keep secrets in a manager, inject at runtime, rotate, and prefer short-lived workload identity.
  • TLS everywhere; envelope encryption for sensitive fields.
  • Use SecureRandom for tokens, constant-time comparison, and mask PII in logs.
api-secrets.body:
Password storage — never encrypt passwords (encryption is reversible); hash them with a slow, salted, adaptive algorithm.

Algorithm Status
Argon2id OWASP's first recommendation (memory-hard)
scrypt good (memory-hard)
bcrypt widely used and fine (cost ≥ 10; input limited to 72 bytes)
PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 acceptable with high iteration counts (FIPS environments)
MD5 / SHA-1 / SHA-256 alone never: fast hashes are brute-forced on GPUs
Java
// Spring Security: the delegating encoder stores the algorithm id with the hash, so you can upgrade later
PasswordEncoder encoder = PasswordEncoderFactories.createDelegatingPasswordEncoder();   // bcrypt by default
String stored = encoder.encode("correct horse battery staple");   // "{bcrypt}$2a$10$..."
boolean ok = encoder.matches(rawFromLogin, stored);
// Argon2 directly: new Argon2PasswordEncoder(16, 32, 1, 1 << 14, 2)  or  Argon2PasswordEncoder.defaultsForSpringSecurity_v5_8()

Secrets management

  • Never commit secrets (pre-commit hooks and secret scanning like gitleaks or GitHub secret scanning). Never bake them into images.
  • Store them in a secrets manager (HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager / SSM Parameter Store, GCP Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault). Inject at runtime via environment variables, mounted files, or Spring Cloud integrations; Kubernetes Secrets are only base64-encoded, so enable etcd encryption and restrict RBAC, or sync from a manager (External Secrets Operator).
  • Prefer short-lived, dynamic credentials (Vault database secrets engine, IAM roles for service accounts / workload identity) over long-lived static passwords.
  • Rotate regularly and immediately after exposure; design apps to reload credentials without restarts where possible.

Encryption

Envelope encryption — how KMS-backed encryption of data at rest works:

  • In transit: TLS 1.2+ everywhere, including inside the cluster (mTLS via a service mesh for zero-trust networks).
  • At rest: disk/volume encryption (managed by the cloud) plus field-level encryption for the most sensitive columns (envelope encryption: data keys encrypted by a KMS master key).
  • Tokens and ids: generate with SecureRandom (or UUIDv4 / UUIDv7 for ids); compare secrets with constant-time comparison (MessageDigest.isEqual).
Java
SecureRandom rnd = new SecureRandom();
byte[] token = new byte[32];
rnd.nextBytes(token);
String resetToken = Base64.getUrlEncoder().withoutPadding().encodeToString(token);
// store only a hash of the reset token (SHA-256 is fine for high-entropy random tokens), with an expiry

Protect personal data in logs: mask PAN, card numbers, phone numbers and emails before logging (Logback masking patterns or structured logging with a sanitizer), never log request bodies wholesale at INFO, and set retention limits.

qa.q: What's the difference between PUT and PATCH, and which is idempotent?
qa.a: PUT replaces the whole resource with the representation sent and is idempotent: sending it twice leaves the same state. PATCH applies a partial modification; it may or may not be idempotent depending on the operation (setting a field is, incrementing is not). Use JSON Merge Patch for simple partial updates.

401 Unauthorized means the request isn't authenticated (no token, expired or invalid token) and should include a WWW-Authenticate header. 403 Forbidden means the caller is authenticated but not allowed to perform the action. Some APIs return 404 instead of 403 to avoid revealing that a resource exists.

qa.q: How do you make a POST endpoint safe to retry?
qa.a: Require an Idempotency-Key header. Store the key per client with a hash of the request and the final response, inserted atomically with a unique constraint before processing. On a retry with the same key and body, return the stored response; with a different body return 422; if the original is still processing return 409. Expire keys after a retention window and pass idempotency keys to downstream providers too.

qa.q: How would you version a public API?
qa.a: Evolve compatibly as long as possible (additive changes, tolerant readers, open enums). For breaking changes, introduce a new major version, usually in the URI, run both versions side by side, communicate a timeline with Deprecation and Sunset headers and documentation, monitor old-version traffic, and retire it once consumers have moved. Guard against accidental breaks with OpenAPI diff checks and contract tests.

qa.q: Offset or cursor pagination for an infinite-scroll feed?
qa.a: Cursor pagination: it uses an index seek on the last seen sort key, so every page has constant cost, and it doesn't produce duplicates or gaps when new items arrive. Offset pagination gets slower for deep pages and shifts when data changes. Return an opaque cursor and a hasMore flag instead of total counts.

qa.q: When would you choose gRPC over REST?
qa.a: For internal service-to-service calls where you control both sides and want a strict schema, low latency and small binary payloads, streaming, and generated clients in many languages. REST stays better for public and browser-facing APIs, HTTP caching, and broad tooling. Note gRPC needs L7 or client-side load balancing because of long-lived HTTP/2 connections.

qa.q: Explain the OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code flow with PKCE.
qa.a: The client creates a random code_verifier and sends its SHA-256 hash (code_challenge) when redirecting the user to the authorization server. After login, the server redirects back with a one-time authorization code. The client exchanges the code plus the original code_verifier at the token endpoint for access, refresh and ID tokens. PKCE ensures an intercepted code is useless without the verifier, and the state parameter protects the redirect from CSRF.

qa.q: What must a resource server validate in a JWT?
qa.a: The signature with a key from the trusted issuer's JWKS (selected by kid), an allowlisted algorithm (never none, no RSA/HMAC confusion), the issuer, that the audience includes this API, and the time claims exp and nbf with small clock-skew leeway. Then check scopes or roles for the endpoint and do object-level authorization.

qa.q: How do you revoke a JWT before it expires?
qa.a: JWTs are self-contained, so you can't un-issue them. Keep access tokens short-lived, rotate refresh tokens and revoke them at the authorization server, and for urgent revocation keep a deny-list of token ids (jti) or user ids with a revocation timestamp in a fast store until the tokens' natural expiry. For high-risk operations use opaque tokens with introspection.

qa.q: What is IDOR and how do you prevent it?
qa.a: Insecure Direct Object Reference: an endpoint accepts an object id and returns or modifies the object without checking that the caller may access it, so users can read others' data by changing ids. Prevent it by scoping every query to the caller or tenant (findByIdAndOwnerId), centralizing authorization checks, denying by default, and writing tests that access other users' objects.

qa.q: Does CORS protect my API from attackers?
qa.a: No. CORS is enforced by browsers to decide whether a web page from another origin may read your responses. Attackers using curl or scripts ignore it entirely. It prevents malicious websites from reading data with your users' credentials in their browsers, which is why you must never combine credentials with a wildcard or reflected origin. Real protection comes from authentication and authorization.

qa.q: When do you need CSRF protection?
qa.a: When the browser authenticates automatically, i.e. with cookies (session cookies, BFF patterns). A malicious site can make the browser send a state-changing request with those cookies attached. APIs that only accept bearer tokens in the Authorization header aren't exposed, because browsers don't add that header by themselves. Use CSRF tokens and SameSite cookies, and never change state on GET.

As salted hashes from a slow, adaptive algorithm designed for passwords: Argon2id, scrypt or bcrypt (or PBKDF2 with many iterations when FIPS is required). Never plain text, never reversible encryption, never fast hashes like SHA-256 alone. Spring's DelegatingPasswordEncoder records the algorithm so hashes can be upgraded later.

qa.q: How do you prevent SSRF in a webhook or URL-import feature?
qa.a: Allowlist permitted hosts or schemes where possible; otherwise resolve the hostname and block private, loopback and link-local ranges (including cloud metadata addresses), re-validate after each redirect or disable redirects, set short timeouts and response size limits, send requests through an egress proxy, and harden the cloud metadata service (IMDSv2).

cheat.api-cheatsheet:
REST resource design, methods and status codes

  • Resources are nouns; methods have defined safety and idempotency (PUT/DELETE idempotent, POST not).
  • Use status codes deliberately: 201 + Location, 202 for async, 409, 412, 422, 429 with Retry-After.
  • Never return 200 with an error body.
  • Allowlist and index filter and sort fields; cap page sizes.

Error responses with Problem Details (RFC 9457)

  • Use RFC 9457 Problem Details (application/problem+json) with stable type URIs.
  • Give every error a machine-readable code and a trace id.
  • Never leak stack traces or internals.
  • Map exceptions centrally; list all validation errors at once.

Pagination, bulk operations and long-running requests

  • Cursor pagination is constant-cost and stable; offset allows page jumps but degrades.
  • Use opaque cursors encoding the last sort key; fetch limit + 1 to compute hasMore.
  • Bulk endpoints should report per-item results and cap batch size.
  • Long-running work returns 202 with a status resource or webhooks.

Idempotency keys, ETags and HTTP caching

  • Idempotency keys make unsafe requests retry-safe: store key + request hash + response.
  • Same key, different body → 422; still in progress → 409; completed → replay.
  • ETags with If-Match give optimistic concurrency (412 on conflict).
  • Cache-Control, ETag and If-None-Match save bandwidth and server work.

Versioning, evolution and API contracts

  • Additive changes are compatible; removing, renaming or retyping fields is not.
  • Version in the URI (most common), header/media type, or by date.
  • Announce retirement with Deprecation and Sunset headers.
  • OpenAPI diff checks and consumer-driven contracts catch breaking changes in CI.

REST vs gRPC vs GraphQL vs WebSockets and SSE

  • REST for public/browser APIs and caching; gRPC for internal low-latency typed calls; GraphQL for client-shaped graphs.
  • Never reuse protobuf field numbers; mark removed ones reserved.
  • Always set gRPC deadlines; balance load at L7 or client-side.
  • SSE for server-to-client streams; WebSockets for bidirectional, with a pub/sub backplane.

Authentication: sessions, OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect

  • Sessions are easy to revoke but need CSRF protection; bearer tokens suit APIs.
  • Use Authorization Code + PKCE for user apps and Client Credentials for services; Implicit and ROPC are deprecated.
  • OIDC adds ID tokens for authentication on top of OAuth 2.0.
  • For SPAs, keep tokens server-side in a BFF and give the browser an HttpOnly cookie.

JWT in depth: structure, validation and pitfalls

  • JWT payloads are readable; never store secrets in them.
  • Validate signature via JWKS, an allowlisted alg, issuer, audience, exp/nbf.
  • Keep access tokens short-lived; rotate refresh tokens; use deny-lists for emergencies.
  • Asymmetric algorithms (RS256/ES256) let many services verify without sharing a secret.

OWASP Top 10 risks in Java backends, with fixes

  • Broken access control (IDOR) is #1: scope every lookup to the caller or tenant.
  • Parameterize all queries; allowlist identifiers like sort columns.
  • Block SSRF by allowlisting hosts and rejecting private and metadata IPs after resolution.
  • Avoid unsafe deserialization, disable XML DTDs, lock down actuator endpoints, scan dependencies.

CORS, CSRF, cookies and security headers

  • CORS is browser-enforced: allowlist explicit origins; never reflect origins with credentials.
  • CSRF matters for cookie-based auth; bearer-token APIs aren't exposed.
  • Session cookies: Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite, optionally the __Host- prefix.
  • Send HSTS, CSP, nosniff and a referrer policy.

Secrets, password storage and encryption

  • Hash passwords with Argon2id, scrypt or bcrypt — never fast hashes or encryption.
  • Keep secrets in a manager, inject at runtime, rotate, and prefer short-lived workload identity.
  • TLS everywhere; envelope encryption for sensitive fields.
  • Use SecureRandom for tokens, constant-time comparison, and mask PII in logs.
